AI firms and the US government are competing for capital:

US Treasury issuance excluding T-bills has risen to $5.06 trillion over the last 12 months, the highest since the 2021 record.

Over the same period, corporate debt issuance has surged to a record $2.64 trillion.

This brings total Treasury and corporate debt issuance up to $7.70 trillion, an all-time high.

This is increasingly driven by AI-related firms, whose bond issuance has soared +541% YoY in 2025, to $109 billion, and another +78% in the first half of 2026, to a record $194 billion.

In other words, corporate America is funding one of the largest investment cycles in decades while the US government is running historically high deficits, forcing both public and private borrowers to compete for capital.

This competition is adding to other forces pushing long-term yields higher, including inflation, Fed policy, and economic growth expectations.

The US bond market is entering an era of intense capital competition.

BREAKING: US median household income adjusted for inflation rose +$2,250 YoY in 2025, or +2.6%, to a record $87,460.

This marks the 3rd consecutive annual increase, totaling +$6,000, or +7.4%.

At the same time, the top 10% saw real income rise +$4,400 YoY, or +1.7%, to a record +$261,300.

This comes as rising stock-market wealth and low unemployment more than offset persistent inflation throughout 2025.

On the other hand, the bottom 10% posted a -$160 YoY decline, or -0.8%, to $20,010.

Furthermore, females earned ~84% as much as their male counterparts last year, up from ~81% in 2024, marking the largest annual increase in the female-to-male earnings ratio in data going back to the early 1960s.

Inflation is being partially offset by higher wages.

The AI trade is undergoing a massive reversal:

The AI Beneficiaries Index relative to the AI At Risk Index has fallen -46% from its late 2025 peak to near its lowest since early 2025.

AI Beneficiaries include semiconductors, tech hardware, and capital-goods companies involved in AI infrastructure such as Nvidia, $NVDA, AMD, $AMD, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Broadcom, $AVGO.

At the same time, AI At Risk includes software and commercial-services companies such as Adobe, $ADBE, Salesforce, $CRM, and ServiceNow, $NOW.

In other words, companies previously expected to benefit from AI have seen the largest drawdown on record relative to companies considered vulnerable to AI disruption.

This comes as investors are increasingly looking beyond AI CapEx and infrastructure, focusing on whether companies can generate tangible benefits from AI, including productivity gains and revenue growth.

This shift also helps explain the turnaround in software stocks, as the group has gone from being viewed as AI's biggest casualty to increasingly being seen as an AI beneficiary itself.

The market is reassessing the winners and losers of AI.

BREAKING: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -403,000 barrels last week, to 285 million barrels, its lowest since November 1982.

This marks the 25th consecutive weekly decline, the longest streak since the 2021-2023 period.

Over this time, US oil inventories in the SPR have dropped -131 million barrels, or -46%.

To put this into perspective, oil reserves in the SPR stood at 650 million barrels in 2020, or +128% above the current levels.

Meanwhile, commercial crude oil stocks excluding the SPR declined -640,000 barrels last week, to 423.4 million barrels, the lowest reading since the end of July.

America's oil reserves are running dangerously low.

Just to add some more context. 

The new relief is not exclusively aimed at crypto. It applies broadly to qualifying providers of "passive software," including interfaces offering access to event contracts, perpetual contracts and other CFTC-regulated derivatives. 

However, because it originated from the Phantom case and expressly covers wallet-based access, it is clearly relevant to crypto developers.

The SEC and CFTC are stepping up to address all major points the crypto industry needed clarity about.

I am sure most of you saw the SEC's innovation exemption today, but the CFTC also released something important that may have gone under the radar: 

Partial protection for software developers, an issue many viewed as central to the CLARITY Act.

In practice, providers of "passive software," including qualifying self-custodial wallets and trading interfaces, can allow users to access CFTC-regulated markets without being required to register as introducing brokers.

To qualify, the developer must remain genuinely passive: it cannot custody user assets, generate explicit buy or sell signals, exercise discretion over order routing or execution, or otherwise control the user's trades. The transactions must also take place through CFTC-registered exchanges, brokers or futures commission merchants.

This expands the relief previously granted specifically to Phantom and makes it broadly available to qualifying software providers.

It is important, however, not to overstate it. This is a CFTC staff no-action position, not legislation, and it does not provide the comprehensive developer safe harbor contemplated under the CLARITY Act. It does not resolve potential DOJ or FinCEN liability under federal money-transmission laws, bind the SEC or state regulators, or necessarily protect developers operating interfaces for unregistered DeFi markets.

Still, alongside the SEC's announcement, it shows that regulators are already using their existing authority to implement meaningful pieces of the framework that Congress failed to pass.
